html:
The Akan are a group of peoples of the forest of southern Ghana and eastern Ivory Coast, who speak related languages such as Twi and Fante. The map shows their lands from 1492 to 1700.

Their forest held some of the richest gold fields in Africa. From about the 1000s the state of Bonoman, at the forest edge, traded gold north to the Mande merchants of the Mali Empire. When the Portuguese built Elmina Castle on the coast in 1482, Akan gold began to flow south as well, and Europeans named the coast the Gold Coast.

The trade brought guns and, later, demand for captives, and larger states formed:

  • Denkyira and Akwamu became powerful in the 1600s;
  • the Fante states controlled much of the coast;
  • in 1701 the Asante threw off Denkyira's rule and became the greatest Akan power.

Akan society traced descent through the mother, used finely made brass weights to measure gold dust, and is known for kente cloth and the Golden Stool, the symbol of Asante kingship.
